intro: A high B♭ calls into silence at the start of Oiseaux tristes. Ravel’s birds sing above slow, uneasy piano figures, with a brief flurry of flight in the middle.

sections.label: A · A solitary B♭
sections.mNote: The upper call begins without accompaniment

sections.label: B · E major and answering calls
sections.mNote: Louder calls have quiet echoes over the moving left hand

sections.label: A′ · The call returns in D minor
sections.mNote: The short–long call returns above held chords

sections.label: Cadenza · Quiet runs without bar lines
sections.mNote: The pianist stretches the rising and falling figures

sections.label: Link · Three measured bars
sections.mNote: The original pace returns and stops under a fermata

sections.label: Coda · Low E♭, distant calls
sections.mNote: Slower still: the piano returns to E♭ minor

cues.title: One bird, no accompaniment
cues.text: A high B♭ repeats, very softly, then opens into a small flourish. The left hand waits for three bars. When it begins, its quavers move in threes beneath the upper part’s twos, keeping the bird’s call slightly apart from its surroundings.
cues.evidence: Miroirs, Demets edition (1906), p. 10: opening B♭, left-hand rests and simultaneous 4/4 and 12/8. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP02693-Ravel-Miroirs,DemetsEd.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Viñes at the Salle Érard
cues.text: The dedication belongs to Ricardo Viñes. On 6 January 1906, at the Salle Érard in Paris, he gives the first performance of all five Miroirs. The pianist who receives these solitary birds also has to launch the ocean and the Spanish dance.
cues.evidence: Dedication, première date, venue and pianist: https://imslp.org/wiki/Miroirs,_M.43_(Ravel,_Maurice).

cues.title: E♭ becomes D♯
cues.text: E♭ is rewritten as D♯, the same piano key with a new destination: E major. A rolled chord opens a fuller passage. High calls sound forte, then answer themselves softly, marked lointain — far away.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 10–11: four-sharp signature, rolled chord and f/pp calls. The E♭–D♯ reinterpretation is described at https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ravel on his birds
cues.text: Ravel dictates that Oiseaux tristes, the first of the five pieces in date and in his view the most typical, strikes him as “birds lost in the torpor of a very dark forest in the hottest hours of summer”.
cues.evidence: Ravel’s notes dictated to Roland-Manuel, 10 October 1928 (BnF, Gallica btv1b10073212x, sheets 6–7): “Le premier en date de ces morceaux et le plus typique de tous est à mon sens le second du recueil: les Oiseaux tristes”, and on the next sheet “des oiseaux perdus dans la torpeur d’une forêt très sombre aux heures les plus chaudes de l’été”. Our translation. Roger Nichols quotes the same image: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W5434_67731

cues.title: Flight without bar lines
cues.text: Ravel removes the bar lines for a quiet cadenza. Slurred runs climb and turn over a slower line below. Lent, presque ad lib. gives the pianist room to linger; even the fastest notes stay at ppp.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, p. 13, first three systems: unbarred cadenza, Lent, presque ad lib. and ppp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The forest grows still
cues.text: The music returns to E♭ minor over a low held E♭. Ravel asks for an even slower pace, sombre et lointain, dark and distant. Short calls linger above the bass, then dwindle under perdendo.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, p. 13, final system: six-flat signature, low E♭, Encore plus lent, sombre et lointain and perdendo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: One pitch turns towards E major
transitions.to: B · E major and answering calls
transitions.how: A short 2/4 bar brings the opening to a close. E♭ becomes D♯, now the leading note of E major, and four sharps replace six flats. A rolled right-hand chord, marked expressif, sounds over a low held bass; rising left-hand notes follow.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition (1906), pp. 10–11; harmonic reading: https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.

transitions.title: The call returns above held chords
transitions.from: B · E major and answering calls
transitions.to: A′ · The call returns in D minor
transitions.how: The fast chords subside and Ravel writes revenez au mouvement. A one-flat key signature brings D minor. The opening’s short–long call returns quietly above tied chords, with the pedal held.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, p. 12: return to the original tempo, one-flat signature, held pedal and returning call.

transitions.title: The bar lines disappear
transitions.from: A′ · The call returns in D minor
transitions.to: Cadenza · Quiet runs without bar lines
transitions.how: A short 2/4 bar leads into Lent, presque ad lib.. The piano stays at ppp with the pedal down, but its runs now cross the page without bar lines. A slower left-hand melody moves below the circling right hand.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 12–13: 2/4 bar and unbarred cadenza.

transitions.title: Three bars recover the pulse
transitions.from: Cadenza · Quiet runs without bar lines
transitions.how: The cadenza presses forward slightly, then au mouvement restores the original pace and the bar lines. A rising left-hand figure reaches a held chord beneath a short upper phrase. Three bars swell from p to mf and back, ending under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, p. 13, third and fourth systems.

transitions.title: A low E♭ beneath the birds
transitions.how: After the fermata, the six-flat signature returns. A low E♭ anchors the piano in E♭ minor while the upper calls sound slowly and softly. Ravel marks Encore plus lent, then perdendo as the last phrases fade.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, p. 13, last two systems.

composer.epithet: He made a ballet from two tunes and a snare drum, and gave his war dead a suite of dances.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
